newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Diesel price dive prompts Chinese buyers to default.
newsitem.headline: Diesel price dive prompts Chinese buyers to default.

text.p: Plunging oil prices have prompted some cash-strapped Chinese firms who bought diesel at record high prices to renege on the deals, leaving sellers with stranded cargoes, industry sources said on Wednesday.
Sellers now had to scrutinise their respective contracts to see if they had any legal or other recourse to avoid possible losses, which could amount to millions of dollars.
The losses would be disastrous for traders who rely on chartered vessels because they incurred high demurrage costs in addition to the value of the diesel cargo, the sources said.
"This (default) started about 20 days ago," one trader said. "There are several cargoes floating off China looking for a home. When you've got a huge volatility, it's quite common."
Traders estimated at least four cargoes, totalling 150,000 tonnes, had not been accepted by Chinese end-users. The market last week estimated the volume at up to 400,000 tonnes.
Chinese buyers were caught unawares when diesel prices that peaked at $34.45 a barrel in early December on the back of a surge in Chinese imports plummeted to $25.50/25.60 on Tuesday.
Traders said the price free-fall had not ended as Chinese demand had all but evaporated ahead of the Lunar New Year holidays in early February.
They said Chinese end-users found it extremely difficult to pay at December prices when deals were made at as high as $263 a tonne on a cost-and-freight (c&f) basis to southern China.

The extent of the fall was seen in a deal made late last week when China's state trader Sinochem bought a cargo at $216 a tonne on c&f, prompting a Sinochem source to say that the lower price could spell "trouble for end-users".
Traders estimated that the aggregate loss that Chinese end-users would have to bear due to the price fall could be between $6 million and $16 million.

"Traders have to be careful with certain customers as some of them are not professional and have no sense of responsibility," said a trader familiar with China. "If the market is in their favour, they would go ahead and take the cargo, but if the market is against them they would flake."
Another trader said sellers who obtained letters of credit (LCs) from Chinese buyers would have little to worry about.
"You just cash in on the LC, it's simple enough. But if the vessel is late, you can cash in on the LC but you bid farewell on the demurrage," he said.
He said those without LCs would face difficulties. "There is nothing much they could do, you can sue the guy, but he would just fold the company if it's a two-dollar company," the trader said.
He said a lot also depended on whether a contract was based on English or Chinese law. The sellers who had based their contracts on Chinese law could have limited legal recourse.
The trader said a legal suit might damage goodwill, but if the transaction amounted to $5 million-$10 million, "you must get yourself covered first and don't worry about future earnings".

Traders said foreign firms were not averse to taking legal action if the amount involved was huge, citing a suit by Lehman Brothers against state-owned Unipec involving a $44 million dispute over currency and swap option trading.
The suit in November 1994, followed by Unipec's counter-suit, was settled last September but revealed the sometimes unorthodox ways in which Chinese companies deal with foreigners.
